nodes.name: Rain and sea mist
nodes.desc: Moist ocean air rising over the Serra do Mar slopes brings heavy rain to the escarpment forests, which keeps them lush.

nodes.name: Warm sunlight
nodes.desc: Year-round warmth and light in the subtropical latitudes support tall, layered forest growth.

nodes.name: Forest soil nutrients
nodes.desc: Nutrients in the soil and leaf litter are recycled quickly in the warm, wet forest and feed the trees.

nodes.name: Fungi and termites
nodes.desc: Break down fallen leaves, fruit and dead animals and return nutrients to the forest soil.

nodes.name: Juçara palm
nodes.desc: An Atlantic Forest palm harvested for heart of palm until it became uncommon. Its fruits are a food for forest birds and mammals.

nodes.name: Fig trees
nodes.desc: Fig trees bear fruit that fruit-eating bats, birds and primates eat. Ficus luschnathiana is among the well-recorded plants here.

nodes.name: Miconia shrubs and trees
nodes.desc: Small-fruited melastome plants that are common in the forest understory. GloBI records show many bats, birds and mammals feeding on their fruit.

nodes.name: Laurels
nodes.desc: Trees of the laurel family, among the most recorded plants in the area (Cryptocarya moschata). Their fleshy fruits are eaten by forest animals.

nodes.name: Myrcia trees
nodes.desc: Myrtle-family trees and shrubs with small berries. Many birds are recorded eating Myrcia fruit.

nodes.name: Southern muriqui
nodes.desc: The largest primate in the Americas, eating mainly fruit plus leaves and flowers. Wikipedia says it has a major role in seed dispersal.

nodes.name: Lowland tapir
nodes.desc: A large browser and fruit eater. Wikipedia says tapirs are important seed dispersers, and large cats are among their main predators.

nodes.name: White-lipped peccary
nodes.desc: A herd-living forest pig that eats fruits, seeds and roots and is prey for jaguars and pumas.

nodes.name: Black capuchin
nodes.desc: A monkey that eats fruit, seeds and other foods. GloBI records it feeding on Miconia and Psychotria fruit, and pumas prey on it.

nodes.name: Great fruit-eating bat
nodes.desc: A fruit bat that feeds on figs and other fruit and carries the seeds away at night.

nodes.name: Red-breasted toucan
nodes.desc: A large-billed bird that swallows fruit whole, including palm fruit, and drops the seeds away from the parent plant.

nodes.name: Cursor grass mouse
nodes.desc: A common small forest rodent, one of the most frequently recorded mammals here. It feeds on seeds, fruit and insects.

nodes.name: Big-eared opossum
nodes.desc: An omnivorous marsupial that eats fruit and small animals. GloBI records show it eating many of the same fruits as other forest animals.

nodes.name: Black vulture
nodes.desc: A common scavenger that cleans up carcasses, including opossums in GloBI records.

nodes.name: Jararaca
nodes.desc: A venomous pit viper of the Atlantic Forest, ambushing small mammals and frogs. It is the most recorded snake in the area.

nodes.name: Jaguar
nodes.desc: The largest cat of the Americas and a top predator here. GloBI links it to tapirs and white-lipped peccaries as prey.

nodes.name: Puma
nodes.desc: A widespread big cat. GloBI links it to black capuchins and white-lipped peccaries, and cougars are listed as tapir predators.
